general.title_original: The Weeklong Attention Span: Thai Society, Violence, and the Shooting Case at Debsirin Nonthaburi School
general.summary_original:
​If we are honest with ourselves, Thai society is one where trending news topics, based on my observation as a journalist over the years, have an average lifespan of about 3 days, or at most about 7 days, and rarely exceed a week. Then the news cycle moves on.

​The role of mainstream mass media as gatekeepers—the sole entities deciding what is or is not news and which angle to take on an issue—has significantly declined over the past decade. This is due to the fact that every ordinary person can now express various opinions on social media, and a considerable number of social media influencers now hold power in sparking social debate.

In this state of extreme chaos, expecting the public to simply shut up, remain passive, and wait for the police or the courts to explain the factors that led to last Friday’s tragedy is inadequate. The 14-year-old gunman first shot his two grandparents to death, went to school, killed six more people—mostly teachers at Debsirin Nonthaburi School—and then shot himself. Waiting is too slow for a society with such a short attention span.

​After a week passes, the number of people still interested in the issue will drop drastically, to the point where almost no one not directly involved will still care or talk about it. Do you still remember the beer house fire in Lat Phrao? Yesterday, another person died from injuries sustained in the fire, bringing the death toll to 38. Is anyone still trying to debate and learn so society can prevent similar incidents? What about the train collision with a bus at Makkasan intersection, which now seems a distant memory despite having occurred just a few months ago?

​In a society with a very short attention span, the first 3–7 days are crucial for collective social learning.

​Please keep an open mind and avoid rushing to a single, simplistic conclusion. Some want the tragedy to have a touching ending and are fixated on the father of a 12-year-old victim, who forgave the perpetrator—despite the fact that the partner of another victim, a mathematics teacher, sobbed and said he “could not come to terms with it”. Meanwhile, a male student from the school released a video clip defending his school and teachers while condemning the shooter, even as some expressed sympathy for the adolescent gunman and blamed certain teachers for allegedly treating him unfairly. But how do we explain the fact that the young gunman killed his own grandparents who had effectively acted as the de facto parents when his biological parents reportedly saw him only on weekends?

Some saw the 14-year-old gunman as a monster; others saw him as a victim. I think I see both, but I will continue to keep my mind open beyond the seven-day mark, which falls tomorrow.

​Keep an open mind, because a flawed society with a limited attention span usually only has 3 to 7 days to learn and debate before moving on.

​Within that short window of public attention, the government also wants to appear resolute, sometimes making knee-jerk reactions.

​Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul controversially said a few days ago that using a gun for self-defence at home is wrong.

​The controversy comes days after the PM said authorities would tighten gun control. Also, the government prohibits state officials from carrying firearms in public or outside their homes when they are not on duty.

On Wednesday, a police spokesman had to explain that an intruder entering a home does not necessarily mean the homeowner can just shoot them in every circumstance, as the force used must be proportionate to the threat.

​Pol Lt Gen Trairong Piwpan explained that there is no blanket rule, and that shooting an intruder does not automatically make the homeowner criminally liable, as each case must be assessed based on the circumstances.

​To Anutin’s embarrassment, records show that seven Bhumjaithai MPs own guns—including Nakhon Phanom MP Anucha Sasomsab, who declared in his asset disclosure, that he possesses as many as 40 guns. Anutin himself has said he once owned a gun but lost it, while his wife has also declared firearms among her assets.

​Yes, Thailand should try to close all the loopholes. More than 10 million guns among a population of about 70 million is one too many. Gun control, as well as reducing the number of firearms, is the way forward. One hopes the government will see to it eventually, but who will keep monitoring it?

Bullying and academic pressure are also factors that must be addressed, although we cannot conclude with certainty at this stage what exact roles they played in the Debsirin Nonthaburi School shooting case. It is amply clear that there have been reports of bullying in other cases, and effective measures are needed.

School security standards should be raised, and young people’s mental well-being should also be addressed.

Following last week’s school shooting, Paul Handley—author of the well-known banned book The King Never Smiles and a prominent foreign observer of Thailand—exchanged views with me on X.

​Handley said he sees Thai society as very violent:

​“Honestly, most Thais also don’t see their society as violent. But it is very violent, and one reason for that is the corrupt police and justice system. The gun problem has been around for a long time, and it is a very serious one.”

​After reading Handley’s post, I replied that I concur in the sense that superficial conflict avoidance and the myth of Thai smiles deter or suppress overt conflicts up to a point, but things can eventually explode violently if people fail to address the thinly concealed anger boiling beneath the surface.

​Later, I reflected further about this. Thai society is a repressed society that places great importance on saving face, conflict avoidance, and maintaining peace and order on the surface level. At the same time, it is an authoritarian society where, once repression reaches a certain point and people can no longer endure it, they may attempt to ‘solve problems’ through an explosion of brutal violence.

Buriram man, 71, beats neighbour to death after years of insults

While I do not yet know for certain whether this applies to this specific case, I think the issue of underlying violence in Thai society is worth serious attention.

​By the way, a military coup is also a way of ‘solving’ political ‘problems’ through violence. They have more than enough guns to overthrow any elected government.

general.title_original: ‘Speak Thai in Thailand’: Psi Scott’s message to foreign workers
general.summary_original:
Thai marine conservationist Psi Scott has sparked an online debate after criticizing foreign service workers in Bangkok for speaking English to Thai customers.

Psi, also known as Sai Samut, shared his views on X through his personal account, @psisamutt, saying he chooses to respond in Thai when foreign employees address him in English.

“If they can’t respond in Thai, I ask to change the person taking my order,” he wrote.

Psi said he believes this is a small way he can encourage the use of Thai in Thailand.

“I’m in Thailand — I want to speak Thai. They can find jobs in Thailand but can’t speak Thai. That is taking advantage of our country,” he wrote.

general.title_original: Invasive blackchin tilapia caught in large numbers off Chonburi coast
general.summary_original:
CHONBURI — 14 August 2026, A local fisherman in Chonburi was shocked after hauling up about 200 kilogrammes of blackchin tilapia in his fishing net off the coast of Rong Po in Bang Lamung district, raising concerns among local fishermen about possible impacts on marine ecosystems and mussel farms.

The incident occurred in the sea off Ban Bang Lamung, also known locally as Rong Po Bay, near the mouth of Bang Lamung Canal in Moo 4, Bang Lamung subdistrict.

A video posted on Facebook showed the fisherman pulling up his net, which was filled with blackchin tilapia (Sarotherodon melanotheron). The man wrote: “I went out to catch fish for dinner… but look what I found.”

The footage attracted attention among local residents.

At 10:00 on 14 August, reporters visited Ban Rong Po beach, a local fishing community, and spoke with the fisherman who posted the video, 27-year-old Natthakorn Suea-iam, known locally as “Tai Nut”.

He said the incident happened on 12 August, when he took his boat out to set nets for grey mullet, intending to bring the fish home to prepare a meal for his family.

When he hauled in the nets, however, he found that almost the entire catch consisted of blackchin tilapia. The fish filled the boat, with the total catch estimated at about 200kg.

Natthakorn said he was shocked because he had spent his life around the sea and had never encountered such a large number of blackchin tilapia in the area.

He said he had previously heard about problems involving the invasive fish species in other parts of Thailand, but had never experienced the problem himself until now.

After bringing the fish ashore, Natthakorn posted a video inviting local residents who needed food to take some of the fish. Many residents subsequently came to collect them.

He also kept some of the fish to experiment with cooking, including frying them and making sun-dried blackchin tilapia. He said the fish tasted similar to Nile tilapia but had fattier meat.

Natthakorn said he was now concerned about whether the fish could affect the local ecosystem. While he acknowledged that he did not have sufficient scientific information to confirm any impact, he was particularly concerned that not a single other species was caught in the net during the fishing trip.

He speculated that the blackchin tilapia may have moved from Bang Lamung Canal into the sea following heavy rainfall. However, he stressed that this was only a local fisherman’s assumption and that authorities would need to investigate the source and establish the facts.

Local fishermen in Rong Po, many of whom also operate mussel farms alongside their coastal fishing activities, have expressed concern over the large number of blackchin tilapia found in the area.

They fear the species could affect local aquatic resources and coastal ecosystems, as well as mussel-farming areas.

The fishermen are calling on fisheries officials and relevant agencies to urgently survey the area, assess the fish population and distribution, and investigate any potential environmental impacts.

general.title_original: Chinese scam boss arrested in Pattaya over alleged money laundering network
general.summary_original:
CHONBURI — 14 August 2026, police have arrested a Chinese man in Pattaya accused of directing a money-laundering network for scam gangs that processed more than 8.8 million baht, authorities said.

The 30-year-old man, identified only as Zhang, was arrested at a condominium in Nong Prue, Bang Lamung district. He was wanted by Chinese authorities on fraud and money-laundering allegations, police said.

He was also charged in Thailand with overstaying his visa.

Police said Zhang was a senior figure who recruited and directed a network to use ATM cards and bank accounts to withdraw and transfer money obtained through scams, in an effort to obscure the funds’ origin and avoid arrest.

Investigators said Zhang travelled to Thailand in 2023 and 2024 to meet accomplices and use the country as an operational base for the scam network. Members of the group allegedly rotated their personal bank accounts to receive fraud proceeds before others were instructed to make large cash withdrawals.

Police said the network handled more than 1.8 million yuan, or about 8.8 million baht.

According to investigators, Zhang fled China through Japan after learning that Chinese authorities were preparing an arrest warrant. He then allegedly entered Thailand illegally and had been hiding in the country since March 2025.

Crime Suppression Division officers, working with Chon Buri immigration police, located him at the Pattaya condominium and made the arrest.

Police said Zhang confessed during questioning to using Thailand as a base to launder money from scam gangs and to hiding in the country after fleeing Chinese authorities.

He was handed over to immigration police for deportation and further legal proceedings in China.

general.title_original: Israeli ambassador asks Surat Thani to help ensure safety of Israeli visitors
general.summary_original:
SURAT THANI — Israel’s ambassador to Thailand has asked Surat Thani authorities to help ensure the safety and well-being of Israeli tourists, long-term residents and business operators in the province.

Ambassador Alona Fisher-Kamm made the request during a meeting with Surat Thani Governor Jumphot Wannachatsiri and provincial officials at the provincial hall on 13 August.

Fisher-Kamm said most Israelis were law-abiding and well-behaved, while acknowledging that some individuals could commit offences.

She said Israel, like other countries, has both good and bad individuals, adding that social media can sometimes create misunderstandings and make people feel unsafe.

The ambassador asked provincial authorities to contact the Israeli Embassy directly if problems involving Israeli nationals arise so that the two sides can work together to resolve them.

She said Israeli authorities had already provided visitors with basic guidance on Thai customs, culture and local laws, including prohibited activities.

Israel currently has five projects aimed at promoting cooperation in Thailand, including a high-value agricultural development project in Koh Samui, she said.

Fisher-Kamm also said she planned to invite the Surat Thani governor to attend a meeting in Israel in November.

Governor Jumphot said Surat Thani treats tourists from all countries equally and takes legal action against anyone who violates Thai law regardless of nationality.

He said provincial authorities were committed to providing transparent and equal treatment to visitors of all nationalities to ensure they feel safe and have a positive experience in the province.

Jumphot also welcomed potential cooperation with Israel on high-value agriculture, saying Israeli projects could provide useful examples for Surat Thani to study.

He said provincial agencies were ready to coordinate with Israeli businesses and visitors, directing business-related matters to the provincial commerce office, tourism issues to the provincial tourism and sports office, and security concerns to provincial police and immigration authorities.

The two officials exchanged souvenirs before concluding the meeting.

Fisher-Kamm was making her fourth visit to Surat Thani. During the visit, she was scheduled to preside over the opening of Khuan La School in Tha Chang district and meet with the Surat Thani provincial police chief later in the day.
